unit.title: Energy, aero and performance in 2026
unit.summary: Where the battery gives lap time, when the wings open, and how teams develop the car.

lessons.title: Energy across a lap
lessons.objective: Explain where a car deploys and where it harvests.

payload.prompt: Where on a lap does a driver deploy electrical power?

options.text: Mainly on straights and exits to gain top speed or traction.
options.explanation: Right. Deployment helps on straights (speed) and exits (traction).

options.text: Under braking to slow the car.
options.explanation: No. Braking harvests energy; deployment makes the car faster.

options.text: Through the entire lap equally.
options.explanation: No, energy is finite. Teams pick spots where it gains the most.

options.text: Only when overtaking.
options.explanation: Overtake Mode is within one second, but deployment helps solo laps.

explanation.correct: Right. Deploy where it gains time: straights for speed, exits for traction.
explanation.incorrect: Deployment is on straights (speed) and exits (traction). Braking harvests, not deploys.
explanation.sayThisLine: The battery helps on straights and exits.

payload.prompt: Does the FIA set a per-lap electrical power deployment limit?

scene.alt: A 2026 F1 car deploying power on a straight.

explanation.correct: Right. The FIA sets per-lap limits to keep racing fair.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. Teams have an FIA-set budget; they must manage it.

payload.prompt: Match energy concepts to their roles.

pairs.definition: Filling battery via braking and engine power.
Using battery power on straights and exits.

distractorDefinitions: Limiting how fast the car goes.
A penalty for using too much power.

explanation.summary: Harvest (braking), store (battery), deploy (speed). MGU-K is the harvest tool.
explanation.sayThisLine: Harvest under braking, deploy on straights.

lessons.title: Clipping and super-clipping
lessons.objective: Explain why a car slows at the end of a straight.

payload.prompt: What happens when a 2026 car clips?

options.text: The battery is empty; power stops and the car forces a harvest.
options.explanation: Right. Clipping = no electrical help and slowing to recharge.

options.text: The engine shuts off.
options.explanation: No, only the electrical assist stops.

options.text: The car crashes.
options.explanation: No, clipping just means the battery is empty. Safe, but slower.

options.text: A penalty is given.
options.explanation: Clipping is not penalised; it is a strategy consequence.

explanation.correct: Right. Clipping = battery empty. Car loses power and must harvest.
explanation.incorrect: Clipping happens when the battery runs out. The car stops accelerating.

payload.prompt: Is clipping on a straight bad for lap time?

scene.alt: A 2026 F1 car clipping on a straight.

explanation.correct: Right. Clipping kills top speed when you need it most.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. Clipping on straights is bad. Teams aim to clip under braking.

payload.prompt: To avoid clipping at the end of a straight, drivers {{method}} to recharge the battery early.
payload.template: To avoid clipping at the end of a straight, drivers {{method}} to recharge the battery early.

explanation.correct: Right. Lifting off throttle early lets teams recharge before the straight ends.
explanation.incorrect: Lift and coast (easing off early) recharges the battery to avoid clipping.

lessons.title: When to open the wings
lessons.objective: Decide when to hold Straight Mode and when to close it.

payload.prompt: Should a driver close the wings before a high-speed corner?

scene.alt: A 2026 F1 car approaching a fast corner.

explanation.correct: Right. Close (high downforce) for corners.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. Open wings reduce grip. Close them for the corner.

payload.prompt: Can drivers use Straight Mode anywhere on the lap?

scene.alt: A 2026 F1 car with Straight Mode active.

explanation.correct: Right. Straight Mode is zone-restricted per circuit.
explanation.incorrect: Only approved zones. Not the whole lap for safety.

payload.prompt: Match each wing mode to its purpose.

pairs.definition: Low-drag wing setting for speed on straights.
High-downforce wing setting for grip and braking.
More downforce increases grip but also increases drag.

distractorDefinitions: A system that works only on tight circuits.
A penalty for using wings incorrectly.

explanation.summary: Straight Mode = speed, Corner Mode = grip. The driver switches to balance both.
explanation.sayThisLine: Open on straights, close for corners.

lessons.title: One lap on the battery
lessons.objective: Explain qualifying energy limits and how they shape a lap.

payload.prompt: In Q3, one lap left. Push flat-out and clip, or conserve battery?

situation.narrative: Final qualifying lap. 0.15 seconds off pole. Battery at 50%.

options.label: Push flat-out, accept clipping
options.consequence: One perfect lap. Clipping at the end costs little vs gaining 0.15 seconds.
considerations: Maximum power on every straight
Clipping happens during braking (low cost)
One shot at pole

options.label: Conserve battery, stay flush
options.consequence: Safe but too slow. You lose deployment time, miss pole.
considerations: No clipping risk
0.1-second loss from missing deployment
Not enough to beat pole anyway

payload.expertNote: Qualifying: one lap trumps energy planning. Push for pole; clipping is a cost you pay.
payload.sayThisLine: In qualifying, push and clip if you must.

payload.prompt: How does battery strategy differ in a race versus a one-lap qualifier?

situation.narrative: Qualifying: deploy it all for one perfect lap. Races: 70 laps with pit stops.

options.label: Completely different: qual=peak power, race=sustained
options.consequence: Correct. Qualifying is maximize-now. Races are maximize-over-distance.
considerations: Per-lap limit is the same
But strategy intent is totally different
Races need pit-window and stint planning

options.label: Similar: just use less battery per lap
options.consequence: Close, but strategy is fundamentally different.
considerations: True you use less per lap
But the decision-making is different

payload.expertNote: Qualifying battery is maximize-now; races require thinking 70 laps ahead.
payload.sayThisLine: Qual: spend it all. Races: save for when it matters.

payload.prompt: In qualifying, how do you treat the battery?

options.text: Deploy it all for one perfect lap and accept clipping.
options.explanation: Right. Qualifying is one-lap pace; maximize your shot.

options.text: Save it for the race.
options.explanation: Wrong. Each weekend's battery is separate. Qualifying and race are different events.

options.text: Recharge during qualifying to prepare for the race.
options.explanation: No, recharge by all means, but maximize qualifying pace first.

options.text: Use only 50% to be safe.
options.explanation: Too conservative. Qualifying is where you need maximum power.

explanation.correct: Right. Qualifying: one lap, maximum power. Strategy comes in the race.
explanation.incorrect: Qualifying energy strategy is maximize-now. Use what you need for pole.

lessons.title: Power unit politics
lessons.objective: Explain homologation-style upgrades and the ADUO safety net.

payload.prompt: What is ADUO?

options.text: Extra engine upgrades for manufacturers falling behind.
options.explanation: Right. ADUO is a safety net: if you are struggling, more upgrade slots.

options.text: A penalty for exceeding the cost cap.
options.explanation: No, ADUO is an aid, not a penalty.

options.text: A ban on mid-season engine upgrades.
options.explanation: No, ADUO enables extra upgrades for lagging makers.

options.text: A noise regulation rule.
options.explanation: ADUO is about development, not sound.

explanation.correct: Right. ADUO gives struggling engine makers extra development chances.
explanation.incorrect: ADUO is a handicap: if you fall behind, you get extra upgrade opportunities.

payload.prompt: What is PU allocation?

options.text: Limited power-unit parts per year; extras incur grid penalties.
options.explanation: Right. Teams have a quota. Extra engines mean grid penalties.

options.text: An equal budget for all teams.
options.explanation: No, allocation is part count, not budget.

options.text: A system that gives one team more power.
options.explanation: No, PU allocation restricts quantity, not power output.

options.text: A renewable resource that resets each race.
options.explanation: Allocation is per season, not per race.

explanation.correct: Right. PU allocation limits components per season. Extra parts mean grid penalties.
explanation.incorrect: PU allocation is a per-season quota. Taking extra costs you grid places.

payload.prompt: What was the 2026 compression-ratio dispute?

options.text: How to measure engine squeeze fairly: cold or hot?
options.explanation: Right. Some complained cold-only measurement was unfair; FIA clarified both.

options.text: A rule that all engines must have equal compression.
options.explanation: No, compression is not standardised. Debate was about fair measurement.

options.text: A ban on high-compression engines.
options.explanation: No, debate was about measurement, not banning high compression.

options.text: A cost-cap rule.
options.explanation: Compression ratio is technical, not a cost issue.

explanation.correct: Right. 2026 debate: measure compression cold and hot to be fair.
explanation.incorrect: The compression-ratio debate was about measurement standards, not banning anything.

payload.prompt: Match 2026 engine makers to their status.

pairs.definition: Incumbent supplier; McLaren, Williams, Alpine customer teams.
New works team; may get ADUO if early pace lags.
New supplier to Aston Martin; also ADUO-eligible.

distractorDefinitions: Only one engine maker on the grid.
Banned from any upgrades until round 6.

explanation.summary: Mercedes is established; Audi and Honda are new and ADUO-eligible.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 has three engine makers fighting a reset.

lessons.title: Aero development and tunnel time
lessons.objective: Explain ATR, flexi-wings and technical directives.

payload.prompt: What is ATR (aero testing restrictions)?

options.text: Wind-tunnel time on a sliding scale: worse teams get more.
options.explanation: Right. Handicap system: slow teams test more to catch up.

options.text: A ban on testing during races.
options.explanation: No, ATR is season development time allocation.

options.text: Equal testing time for all teams.
options.explanation: Wrong; it is a sliding scale, not equal.

options.text: A requirement to use only one tunnel.
options.explanation: ATR is about time limit, not facility rules.

explanation.correct: Right. ATR is a handicap: finishing last last year = more wind tunnel this year.
explanation.incorrect: ATR is development time allocation on a sliding scale for competitive balance.

payload.prompt: Are flexi-wings (wings that bend during racing) allowed in F1?

scene.alt: A flexi-wing bending under aerodynamic load.

explanation.correct: Right. Flexi-wings are banned, but teams keep trying the loophole.
explanation.incorrect: Flexi-wings are banned, but it is a recurring loophole fight.

payload.prompt: What is a flexi-wing loophole?

options.text: Wings that bend under load to cut drag while passing static tests.
options.explanation: Right. Carbon-fibre wings flex during racing but look rigid in the garage.

options.text: A driver-adjustable wing like active aero.
options.explanation: No, flexi is hidden bending, not intentional adjustment.

options.text: A wing made of rubber.
options.explanation: No, flexi-wings are carbon-fibre that bend strategically.

options.text: A permanent design banned since 2020.
options.explanation: Flexi-wings are not banned permanently; the FIA fights ongoing attempts.

explanation.correct: Right. Flexi-wing: bend in the air for drag cut, look rigid when tested.
explanation.incorrect: A flexi-wing is a structural loophole: bends during racing, passes static tests.

payload.prompt: Match aero loopholes to how the FIA fights back.

pairs.definition: Wing that bends to cut drag while passing static tests.
FIA clarification issued quickly to close loopholes.
Teams find loopholes; FIA closes them mid-season via TDs.

distractorDefinitions: A new wing that is faster than others.
A penalty for using banned components.

explanation.summary: Flexi-wing is the loophole; technical directives close it fast.
explanation.sayThisLine: TDs close loopholes like flexi-wings mid-season.

lessons.title: The cost cap and how teams spend
lessons.objective: Explain the cap and why it matters to competitiveness.

payload.prompt: What is the F1 cost cap?

options.text: Yearly spending limit ($215M) with carve-outs for driver salaries.
options.explanation: Right. Teams have a fixed budget; exceeding it brings penalties.

options.text: An equal budget for all teams.
options.explanation: No, the cap is a limit, not an equal grant.

options.text: A ban on expensive components.
options.explanation: No, the cap limits total spending, not part cost.

options.text: A regulation from the 1980s.
options.explanation: The cost cap started in 2021, not the 1980s.

explanation.correct: Right. Cost cap is roughly $215M per year. Breaches bring penalties.
explanation.incorrect: The cost cap is an annual spending ceiling with sporting penalties for breaches.

payload.prompt: Why does the cost cap matter for grid fairness?

options.text: Prevents the richest teams from outspending everyone.
options.explanation: Right. The cap keeps the grid even against billionaire budgets.

options.text: Reduces car quality and makes racing slower.
options.explanation: Capping spending does not slow cars; teams innovate within limits.

options.text: Forces teams to buy cheaper parts.
options.explanation: The cap limits total spending, not part cost.

options.text: Has no real impact on the grid.
options.explanation: The cap has huge impact: keeps small teams competitive.

explanation.correct: Right. Cost cap prevents unlimited spending from creating a billionaire-only arms race.
explanation.incorrect: The cost cap keeps spending in check so smaller teams stay competitive.

payload.prompt: Guess the F1 cost cap per team per year, in millions of dollars.

explanation.correct: Right. Cost cap is roughly $215M per team per year.
explanation.incorrect: The F1 cost cap is approximately $215 million per year per team.
explanation.sayThisLine: Cost cap is about $215 million per team per year.

payload.prompt: What happens if a team exceeds the cost cap?

options.text: Fines and sporting penalties including points deductions.
options.explanation: Right. FIA fines and can deduct points or ban from races.

options.text: They refund the excess money.
options.explanation: No, penalties are fines and sporting sanctions.

options.text: Nothing; the cap is voluntary.
options.explanation: No, the cap is mandatory with real consequences.

options.text: The driver is banned.
options.explanation: Penalties are team penalties, not driver bans.

explanation.correct: Right. Cost-cap breaches draw fines and sporting penalties.
explanation.incorrect: Teams that exceed the cost cap face fines and point deductions.

lessons.title: Reading pace from practice
lessons.objective: Tell one-lap pace from race pace and spot sandbagging.

payload.prompt: What do Friday long runs tell you about a team's race pace?

situation.narrative: Friday: Team A runs 0.4 seconds slower in the long run than in qualifying simulations.

options.label: Their race pace is weak; expect them to fade
options.consequence: Correct. 0.4 seconds is big. Expect grid-to-finish drop.
considerations: Tyre or balance weakness shows in long runs
Fast Saturday, struggling Sunday likely
Good signal for tracking their form

options.label: Just fuel load; race pace is fine
options.consequence: Partial. Fuel matters but 0.4 seconds signals real pace loss.
considerations: Fuel load is part of it
But 0.4 seconds usually means a handling issue

payload.expertNote: Friday long runs hint at race pace. A 0.4-second gap is significant.
payload.sayThisLine: Long runs show who has race pace.

payload.prompt: How can you spot sandbagging (hidden pace) in practice?

situation.narrative: Friday: Team B is 12th on the timing sheet. Saturday: pole position.

options.label: Deliberate sandbagging: hiding pace with fuel
options.consequence: Correct. 12th to pole is intentional hiding, not just setup.
considerations: Heavy fuel and conservative setup hide one-lap pace
Qualifying setup is totally different
Jump that big signals strategy, not just tyres

options.label: Just tyres and setup differences
options.consequence: Partial. Tyres matter but that gap shows intent.
considerations: Setup does change between Friday and Saturday
But jump that big usually means sandbagging

payload.expertNote: Sandbagging is intentional. Teams run heavy or loose Friday to hide pace.
payload.sayThisLine: Sandbagging: hide pace with fuel and strategy.

payload.prompt: What is the difference between qualifying and race pace?

options.text: Qualifying is one-lap peak; races are consistent speed with tyre management.
options.explanation: Right. Different priorities: qual = peak, race = stamina over 20-30 laps.

options.text: They are the same; fast cars are fast both ways.
options.explanation: No, cars can excel at one but struggle at the other.

options.text: Race pace is always faster because less fuel.
options.explanation: No, light fuel in qualifying is fastest. Race includes fuel weight.

options.text: Only driver matters for qualifying; team matters for races.
options.explanation: Both depend on driver and car. Metrics are just different.

explanation.correct: Right. Qualifying = one-lap flat-out. Race = stamina with tyre and fuel.
explanation.incorrect: Qualifying pace is peak one-lap. Race pace is sustained over a stint.

payload.prompt: A team qualifies 3rd but finishes 6th. What does that tell you?

options.text: Race pace is weaker; they faded from tyre wear or balance.
options.explanation: Right. Grid position vs finish tells the story.

options.text: The driver made a mistake.
options.explanation: Maybe, but a 3-to-6 drop usually points to pace.

options.text: They used wrong tyres.
options.explanation: Possible, but gap suggests a deeper pace issue.

options.text: Nothing; results vary.
options.explanation: A big drop is a clear signal about pace balance.

explanation.correct: Right. Grid-to-finish drop is a red flag for race-pace weakness.
explanation.incorrect: A grid-to-finish drop signals weak race pace versus qualifying.
